_meta.name: Onboarding
_meta.note: Module 02. You cannot spot deviation without first establishing what normal looks like — which is why this precedes any monitoring work. The decision is not 'is this customer a criminal' but 'how much diligence is proportionate, and what should I expect from this account'. Getting the expected profile wrong is what makes every later alert noise.

schema.expected: the profile the analyst sets; wrong settings generate noise later

cases.title: A nurse opening a current account
cases.applicant: Ms F. Bakayoko · individual · Belgian resident
cases.intro: The simplest file you will see. Worth doing carefully anyway, because the profile you set here is what every future alert is measured against.

facts.Initial deposit: €1,400 by transfer from another Belgian bank

documents.s: Verified electronically. Name, DOB and address match the application.
Permanent, university hospital, salary consistent with declared income.
Utility bill, three weeks old, matches eID.

cases.screening: No sanctions match. No PEP match. No adverse media.
cases.why: Everything reconciles and nothing elevates the risk: a domestic salaried individual, verified identity, a product with no unusual features, and a funding source that matches the declared income. Standard due diligence is what proportionality means here — applying enhanced measures to a file like this is not caution, it is a misallocation of the effort that the difficult files need.

outcomes.standard: Correct. Verified, proportionate, and the expected profile is set so future deviations will actually mean something.
outcomes.edd: Enhanced measures on a salaried nurse with a verified eID. Nothing here justifies it, and the hours spent are hours not spent on a file that needed them.
outcomes.more: You already hold identity, address, employment and source of funds. There is nothing further to ask for.
outcomes.decline: You have declined a customer with no risk indicator whatsoever. Beyond the commercial cost, this is the behaviour that produces de-risking of entire customer segments.

cases.law: AMLR Art. 20 — CDD measures proportionate to risk; Art. 25 — the expected profile is what ongoing monitoring measures against.
cases.lesson: Most onboarding is this. The skill being trained is not suspicion — it is setting an accurate expected profile quickly, so that the monitoring system has a meaningful baseline. A profile set carelessly here becomes a false positive every month for the next decade.

cases.title: A logistics company with a holding structure
cases.intro: A real operating business with a perfectly ordinary reason to have a holding company above it. The question is whether you can see all the way to the top.

facts.Activity: Road freight, Benelux and northern France

documents.s: Active since 2011. Registered address matches the depot. Directors named.
Filed, audited, turnover consistent with declared figures.
Bruneel Holding NV owns 100%. Holding is owned by Mr J. Bruneel (62%) and Mrs A. Bruneel (38%), both Belgian residents, named as founders in the 2011 filing.
Authorises the account opening. Signatories match the directors.

cases.screening: No sanctions or PEP match on the company, the holding, or either individual. No adverse media.
cases.why: A holding company above an operating company is one of the most ordinary structures in European business, and its presence is not a risk indicator. What matters is whether you can identify the natural persons at the top — and here you can, from filed documents, with two named Belgian residents holding the whole chain. The structure is transparent, so standard measures are proportionate.

outcomes.standard: Correct. Two layers, but you can see through both to identified natural persons. Transparent structure, ordinary business, proportionate response.
outcomes.edd: Defensible caution, but the presence of a holding company is not itself a red flag. If every corporate structure triggers enhanced measures, enhanced measures stop meaning anything.
outcomes.more: You hold the company extract, the accounts, the ownership chain and a board resolution. Naming what is still missing would be difficult.
outcomes.decline: A profitable Belgian operating company with fully transparent ownership. Declining this is a commercial decision with no compliance basis.

cases.law: AMLR Art. 22 — identification of beneficial owners; Art. 20 — proportionality.
cases.lesson: Layers are not opacity. The test is whether the chain terminates in identified natural persons using documents you can verify. This case exists because analysts trained only on suspicious files start treating ordinary corporate structures as suspicious, and that is its own kind of failure.

cases.title: A consultancy that arrives with a nominee
cases.intro: Two months old, a nominee shareholder, and a projected turnover that would make it immediately profitable. Everything is documented. That is not the same as everything being clear.

facts.Applicant: Ltd, incorporated Malta, two months ago
facts.Activity: Management consultancy, declared clients in three jurisdictions
facts.Ownership: Sole shareholder: Fiducia Corporate Services Ltd (nominee)

documents.s: Valid, Malta Business Registry, dated two months ago.
Single shareholder: Fiducia Corporate Services Ltd, a licensed corporate services provider acting as nominee.
Confirms Fiducia holds on behalf of a beneficial owner, but names no individual. Fiducia states it will disclose only on formal request through its own compliance channel.
Projects €2.8M year-one turnover from three named clients. No signed contracts attached. No prior trading history.
Passport of the sole director, a Maltese resident, verified. He is also a director of eleven other Fiducia-administered companies.

cases.screening: No sanctions or PEP match on the company, the nominee, or the director. No adverse media.
cases.why: Nothing here is illegitimate, and nothing here is established either. You cannot identify the beneficial owner — a nominee declaration that names no individual is precisely the absence of the information Art. 22 requires. Add a director who fronts eleven other companies and projected turnover with no contracts behind it, and you have a file you cannot yet risk-rate at all. This is not a decline: the nominee has said it will disclose through a formal channel, and you have not used it. Ask, then decide.

outcomes.standard: You have onboarded a customer whose beneficial owner is unknown to you. Every monitoring alert on this account will now be assessed against a profile you had no basis to set.
outcomes.edd: Enhanced measures are right in spirit, but they do not substitute for the missing fact. You cannot apply enhanced diligence to a beneficial owner you have not identified — EDD without identification is activity, not diligence.
outcomes.more: Correct. The nominee has a disclosure channel and you have not used it. Nothing can be concluded until the beneficial owner is named, and everything can be concluded quickly once they are.
outcomes.decline: Premature. A nominee arrangement is lawful and common in Malta, and the provider has offered a disclosure route. Declining before asking is how legitimate business gets pushed toward less scrupulous institutions.

cases.law: AMLR Art. 22 — beneficial ownership must be identified, not assumed; Art. 21 — where CDD cannot be completed, the relationship must not be established.
cases.lesson: The hardest onboarding decisions are not between good and bad customers. They are files where nothing is wrong and nothing is proven, and the discipline is refusing to rate a risk you have no basis to rate. Note the trap in both wrong answers: 'standard' and 'decline' are opposite errors made for the same reason — deciding without the fact that decides it.

cases.title: A mayor's business partner
cases.applicant: Devos & Lemmens Architecten BV · corporate · Belgian
cases.intro: An architecture practice with two partners. One of them is married to a sitting mayor. The practice bids for public work.

facts.Ownership: P. Devos (50%), M. Lemmens (50%), both Belgian residents

documents.s: Active since 2018. Both partners named as directors.
Filed and consistent. Roughly 40% of revenue from public-sector clients.
Includes three municipalities. One is the municipality where Mrs Lemmens' spouse serves as mayor.

cases.screening: M. Lemmens is identified as the spouse of a domestic PEP — mayor of a Belgian municipality of 22,000. No sanctions match. No adverse media on any party.
cases.why: A PEP association is not an allegation and the practice appears entirely genuine. But Art. 42 is not discretionary: a family member of a PEP triggers enhanced due diligence, senior management approval, and source-of-wealth establishment. The public-sector revenue makes it material rather than technical — the firm earns from municipalities, one of which the PEP heads, which is exactly the conflict the PEP regime exists to monitor.

outcomes.standard: You have missed a mandatory trigger. Art. 42 requires enhanced measures and senior management approval for a PEP family member — this is a procedural failure an examiner would find in the file, regardless of whether anything improper ever occurs.
outcomes.edd: Correct. Enhanced measures, senior management approval, source of wealth, and closer monitoring of the municipal revenue stream — applied because the rule requires it, not because anything is wrong.
outcomes.more: You have the identification and the accounts. The gap is not information, it is the enhanced process the PEP status obliges you to apply.
outcomes.decline: Declining a legitimate practice because a partner is married to a mayor is exactly the over-reaction the FATF has repeatedly warned against. PEP status requires management, not exclusion.

cases.law: AMLR Art. 42 — PEPs, their family members and close associates: enhanced due diligence, senior management approval, source of wealth, enhanced ongoing monitoring.
cases.lesson: PEP handling is where two opposite failures live side by side. Under-apply and you have a procedural breach on the file. Over-apply and you exclude legitimate customers for an association they did not choose. The regime asks for neither suspicion nor exclusion — it asks for documented, proportionate attention.

profiles.d: Regular monthly credit from one employer, card spend, occasional transfers.
Invoiced income from identified counterparties, supplier payments, payroll.
Regular cash deposits proportionate to a declared trade.
Insufficient information to state what normal activity would look like.
